predictions.explanation:
As of November 30, 2025, the United States has **not** achieved “semiconductor independence” in any reasonable sense:

- Taiwan still dominates advanced-chip foundry capacity. TrendForce estimated that in 2023 Taiwan held ~46% of global foundry capacity and 68% of advanced-process capacity, with nearly 80% of EUV-era (7 nm and below) production; Taiwan is projected to remain the single largest advanced-node base into at least the late 2020s. ([trendforce.com](https://www.trendforce.com/presscenter/news/20231214-11959.html?utm_source=openai))  
- A 2024/2025 U.S. government briefing and subsequent analysis put Taiwan’s share of the most advanced chips at over 90%, with U.S. (largely Silicon Valley) firms as TSMC’s biggest customers and about 70% of TSMC’s 2024 net revenue coming from North America—evidence of continuing U.S. dependence on Taiwanese manufacturing. ([stimson.org](https://www.stimson.org/2025/why-taiwan-fears-america-first-risks-eroding-its-silicon-shield/?utm_source=openai))  
- TSMC’s Arizona fabs have begun producing advanced chips and more U.S. and allied capacity is being added, but reporting in 2025 emphasizes that these facilities are intended to *complement*, not replace, TSMC’s main operations, and that the U.S. remains tightly entangled with Taiwan for leading-edge supply. ([foreignpolicy.com](https://foreignpolicy.com/2025/10/10/tsmc-taiwan-semiconductor-arizona-tech/?utm_source=openai))  
- Analyses of TSMC’s global footprint project that more than 80% of its advanced chips will still be fabricated in Taiwan for at least the next five years, and that Taiwan will retain roughly 58–60% of global advanced fabrication capacity by 2030. ([taiwaninsight.org](https://taiwaninsight.org/2025/05/12/tsmc-the-enduring-silicon-shield-of-taiwans-economy/?utm_source=openai))  
- Independent commentary in 2024 likewise notes that Taiwan produces about 90% of the world’s most advanced semiconductors, underscoring that global (and particularly U.S.) dependence on Taiwanese production remains extremely high. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/world/article/2024/jul/19/taiwan-semiconductor-industry-booming?utm_source=openai))

However, Vivek Ramaswamy’s prediction did **not** include a clear, falsifiable deadline; he spoke about achieving semiconductor independence in a “foreseeable future” relevant to Taiwan defense planning, which plausibly extends well beyond 2025 into the late 2020s or 2030s. Because that implied time horizon has not yet elapsed, we cannot definitively say the prediction has failed—only that it has **not yet come true**.

Given the current date and the open-ended timeframe in the original claim, the appropriate verdict is that it is **too early to tell** whether his prediction will ultimately be right or wrong.

predictions.grok_explanation: The US has not achieved semiconductor independence from Taiwan by December 2025. Taiwan, particularly TSMC, still produces over 90% of the world's most advanced semiconductors (e.g., sub-10nm nodes critical for AI, defense, and modern tech). While CHIPS Act investments have led to progress—e.g., TSMC's Arizona Fab 1 began high-volume N4 production in late 2024 and 4nm/5nm in early 2025, with Fab 2 targeting N3 in 2028—US capacity remains a tiny fraction of needs, and supply chains/expertise are still Taiwan-dependent. Recent reports confirm ongoing strategic vulnerability: Foreign Policy (Oct 2025) states 'the U.S. remains dependent on Taiwan'; SIA '2025 State of the U.S. Semiconductor Industry' emphasizes resiliency goals but not independence; US officials push for Taiwan to cap US chip supply at 50% (Sep/Oct 2025), rejected by Taiwan. Over 2.5 years since the July 2023 prediction, no independence for 'modern way of life' chips, relevant to near-term Taiwan defense planning.

Vivek Ramaswamy ended his 2024 presidential campaign on January 15, 2024, after finishing fourth in the Iowa Republican caucuses, and he endorsed Donald Trump instead of continuing his own bid. Multiple outlets report that he *suspended* his campaign and acknowledged there was “no path” for him to become president. ([cbsnews.com](https://www.cbsnews.com/news/vivek-ramaswamy-drops-out-2024-presidential-race-iowa-caucuses/?utm_source=openai))  

Donald Trump, not Ramaswamy, went on to secure enough delegates to become the 2024 Republican presidential nominee ([people.com](https://people.com/donald-trump-2024-presumptive-republican-presidential-nominee-8605168?utm_source=openai)) and ultimately won the 2024 U.S. presidential election. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election?utm_source=openai))  

Because Ramaswamy neither secured the Republican nomination nor won the general election, his prediction that his own 2024 presidential campaign would be successful in that sense was **wrong**.

predictions.explanation:
B/Vivek Ramaswamy’s prediction had several linked parts:

1. **Be polling at least 3rd nationally (possibly 2nd) by Nov–Dec 2023**  
   Nationwide polling in November–December 2023 consistently showed Ramaswamy running **fourth** in the GOP field, behind Trump, DeSantis, and Haley. For example, a series of national polls summarized by Wikipedia for late November and December 2023 (CNN/SSRS, Monmouth, WSJ, Morning Consult, etc.) all have the ranking Trump 1st, DeSantis and Haley in 2nd/3rd, and Ramaswamy in 4th with mid–single-digit support. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nationwide_opinion_polling_for_the_2024_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries))  A December 23, 2023 summary of FiveThirtyEight’s aggregate cited by *Newsweek* lists Trump at 62.4%, DeSantis 11.7%, Haley 10.8% nationally – with Ramaswamy **below those three**, i.e., not in the top three. ([newsweek.com](https://www.newsweek.com/nikki-haley-donald-trump-2024-gop-primary-challenge-new-hampshire-polls-1855222?utm_source=openai))  
   
   While Ramaswamy had briefly reached 3rd place around August 24, 2023 (10.3% in FiveThirtyEight’s average), by January 14, 2024 he had fallen to 4th at 4.3%, behind Trump, DeSantis, and Haley. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivek_Ramaswamy_2024_presidential_campaign?utm_source=openai))  There is at least one mid‑December McLaughlin poll where he ties Haley at 8%, effectively joint 3rd, but in the *overwhelming majority* of national polls and in the polling averages for Nov–Dec 2023 he was 4th, not clearly 3rd or 2nd.

2. **“Overperform expectations” in Iowa and New Hampshire**  
   - **Iowa caucuses (Jan 15, 2024):** Final polling averages for Iowa shortly before the caucus put Trump >50%, DeSantis and Haley in the mid‑teens, and Ramaswamy around **6–7%**. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Statewide_opinion_polling_for_the_2024_Republican_Party_presidential_primaries?utm_source=openai))  The actual results were Trump 51.0%, DeSantis 21.2%, Haley 19.1%, and Ramaswamy 7.7% (4th place). ([iowastatedaily.com](https://iowastatedaily.com/288114/news/iowa-caucus-results-trump-wins-majority-ramaswamy-drops-out/?utm_source=openai))  That performance was roughly in line with, or slightly below, expectations and was widely described as a disappointing showing; he suspended his campaign that night, explicitly saying there was “no path” forward. ([iowapublicradio.org](https://www.iowapublicradio.org/live-updates/2024-iowa-caucuses?utm_source=openai))  This is the opposite of a clear “overperformance.”
   - **New Hampshire primary (Jan 23, 2024):** By New Hampshire, Ramaswamy had already withdrawn. Official results show Trump at 54.35%, Haley at 43.28%, and Ramaswamy receiving only **0.3%** as a write‑in. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2024/jan/23/new-hampshire-primary-election-results?utm_source=openai))  There was no overperformance or positive momentum to leverage.

3. **Use that momentum to win the 2024 Republican nomination**  
   Instead of gaining momentum, Ramaswamy exited the race immediately after Iowa and endorsed Donald Trump. ([apnews.com](https://apnews.com/article/4b794ed3fbb41cc7f2a6a95d20458843?utm_source=openai))  Trump then dominated subsequent primaries and caucuses, surpassing the delegate threshold to become the **presumptive Republican nominee** on March 12, 2024, and was formally nominated at the Republican National Convention in July 2024. ([pbs.org](https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/trump-clinches-2024-republican-nomination?utm_source=openai))  Ramaswamy never came close to winning the nomination.

Because (a) he was generally **not** in 3rd (let alone 2nd) nationally by November–December 2023 in the polling averages, (b) he did **not** clearly overperform expectations in Iowa or New Hampshire, and (c) he emphatically did **not** win the 2024 Republican nomination, the overall prediction is best judged as **wrong**, even though he briefly reached 3rd place months earlier than the timeframe he named.

predictions.explanation:
Key parts of Sacks’s forecast did not match what ultimately happened:

1. **No Biden–Trump rematch**  
Sacks said “we’re on track to have a Biden–Trump rematch.” In reality, Joe Biden withdrew from the 2024 race on July 21, 2024, and Kamala Harris became the Democratic nominee on August 5, 2024. The general election on November 5, 2024 was **Donald Trump vs. Kamala Harris**, not Biden vs. Trump.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Joe_Biden_from_the_2024_United_States_presidential_election?utm_source=openai))

2. **Biden did not end up the more likely (or actual) winner**  
Sacks also said that, as of July 2023, Biden “probably looks like he’s going to win.” In the actual 2024 election, **Donald Trump defeated Kamala Harris**, winning 312 electoral votes to Harris’s 226 and also winning the national popular vote. Biden was not on the ballot and did not win.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_United_States_presidential_election?utm_source=openai))

3. **His listed “unless” conditions largely did *not* occur before the election**  
   * **Recession:** As of October 3, 2024, the Congressional Research Service reported that the NBER had *not* dated any new peak (and thus no new recession) after the April 2020 trough, meaning the U.S. was still in the same expansion through the 2024 election.([congress.gov](https://www.congress.gov/crs_external_products/IF/HTML/IF10411.web.html?utm_source=openai))  
   * **Ukrainian collapse:** Ukraine suffered serious reverses (e.g., loss of Avdiivka and other territory in 2024), but its military and state did not collapse; by 2024–25 the front had largely stabilized into a long defensive line and Ukraine continued to fight across a ~1,200 km front.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Avdiivka_%282023%E2%80%932024%29?utm_source=openai))  
   * **January 6–related indictment:** A federal indictment related to Trump’s efforts to overturn the 2020 election and the January 6 attack was filed on August 1, 2023 (United States v. Trump).([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Federal_prosecution_of_Donald_Trump_%28election_obstruction_case%29?utm_source=openai))  However, that case never reached a verdict before the election and there is no clear evidence it “significantly” harmed Biden’s electoral prospects; indeed, Biden withdrew for reasons centered on age, performance and political viability, and Trump went on to win the general election against Harris.([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Withdrawal_of_Joe_Biden_from_the_2024_United_States_presidential_election?utm_source=openai))

Because (a) the predicted Biden–Trump rematch did not occur, (b) Biden did not end up the winner, and (c) the specified exception conditions either did not materialize (recession, Ukrainian collapse) or did not clearly play out in the way implied, the overall prediction does **not** match the eventual outcome.

predictions.explanation:
The prediction tied the “tip right” to the **near‑term national election cycle** (the July 23, 2023 Spanish general election) and specified that this meant right‑leaning parties would **gain power or form the governing coalition**.

Here is what happened:

- In the **July 23, 2023 general election**, the centre‑right People’s Party (PP) did win a **plurality** with 137 seats, ahead of the governing Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) with 121 seats. However, the right‑wing bloc (PP + Vox + small allies) fell short of a majority (around 171 seats vs. 176 needed).
- Because the right bloc lacked the numbers, PP leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo was **unable to form a government**.
- Instead, **Pedro Sánchez (PSOE)** was **re‑elected prime minister on 16 November 2023** after securing an absolute majority of 179 MPs with a coalition agreement between the centre‑left PSOE and left‑wing Sumar, backed by several regional/nationalist parties. This produced another **left‑of‑centre coalition government**, not a right‑wing one.
- Subsequent reporting through 2024–2025 still describes Spain as governed by this **PSOE–Sumar coalition under Sánchez**, indicating no later right‑wing takeover within that same electoral cycle.

Because the national government did **not** shift to the right or come under the control of right‑leaning parties during the referenced election cycle, the prediction that “Spain looks like it’s about to tip right” (in the sense of its government changing hands) did **not** come true.
predictions.grok_explanation: The podcast was released on July 21, 2023, just before Spain's snap general election on July 23, 2023. The center-right People's Party (PP) won the most seats (136) and votes, with far-right Vox gaining 33 seats, but they fell short of a majority (176 needed). Incumbent socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez (PSOE) retained power by forming a left-wing coalition government, invested on November 16, 2023. As of December 2025, Sánchez remains PM ([La Moncloa](https://www.lamoncloa.gob.es/lang/en/presidente/biografia/paginas/index.aspx), recent news like [Guardian Nov 30, 2025](https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/nov/30/thousands-rally-in-madrid-to-demand-pm-resign-over-corruption-allegations)). No new general election has occurred (next due by Aug 2027; [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Next_Spanish_general_election)). Right-leaning parties gained seats but did not form the governing coalition, so the government did not shift right ([Wikipedia 2023 election](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Spanish_general_election), [BBC Nov 2023](https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/world-europe-67436378)).

predictions.explanation:
As of 30 November 2025, the war in Ukraine has indeed become prolonged and has not been resolved quickly or cleanly, but it has *not* turned into a Vietnam‑ or Iraq‑style quagmire **for the United States and its allies** in the usual sense of those comparisons.

**Protracted, unresolved conflict:**
- Russia’s full‑scale invasion began in February 2022 and large‑scale fighting continues in late 2025, including ongoing operations like the Pokrovsk offensive (since July 2024) and the Northern Kharkiv front, which has largely stalemated after a major Russian offensive in May 2024. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pokrovsk_offensive?utm_source=openai))
- Ukrainian and Western officials in 2025 describe the situation as a grinding *war of attrition* that could drag on for years, with no decisive victory or comprehensive peace yet in place. ([theguardian.com](https://www.theguardian.com/global/2025/may/18/we-will-pay-a-huge-price-ukraine-fears-war-could-drag-on-for-years?utm_source=openai))
- Multiple diplomatic efforts in 2025 (UN resolutions, the London peace summit, a U.S.-brokered 30‑day ceasefire proposal accepted by Ukraine if Russia agrees) have not yet produced a lasting settlement; deadly missile and drone attacks continue. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_London_Summit_on_Ukraine?utm_source=openai))  
These facts support the part of his prediction that the war would be long and messy rather than “quick or clean.”

**Degree and nature of U.S./ally entanglement:**
- The U.S. is heavily involved via aid and diplomacy. By 2024–25, the U.S. has provided roughly half of all military aid to Ukraine and well over $100 billion in total related spending, and it is central to ceasefire and peace negotiations. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States_and_the_Russian_invasion_of_Ukraine?utm_source=openai))
- However, NATO and independent fact‑checkers consistently state that there are **no NATO combat troops in Ukraine**, and that the alliance has *no plans* to deploy them; Western military support is limited to weapons, training (mostly outside Ukraine), and intelligence/logistics. ([globalsecurity.org](https://www.globalsecurity.org/wmd/library/news/ukraine/2022/ukraine-220224-nato06.htm?utm_source=openai))
- The hallmarks of Vietnam/Iraq‑style quagmires for the U.S.—massive ground deployments, prolonged direct combat by U.S. forces, and large U.S. battle casualties—are absent. The burdens are primarily financial, political, and industrial, with Ukrainians and Russians bearing the direct combat losses. ([en.wikipedia.org](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Casualties_of_the_Russo-Ukrainian_war?utm_source=openai))

Because the **“long, unresolved war”** part of the prediction has clearly materialized, but the **“Vietnam or Iraq‑style quagmire for the United States and its allies”** component has not (no large Western troop deployment or direct-occupation war), the forecast is only partially borne out. That mix of accurate and overstated elements makes the overall assessment **ambiguous** under your scoring scheme.

predictions.grok_explanation: The Ukraine conflict remains ongoing as of December 1, 2025, nearly four years after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022, with active fighting reported (e.g., ISW assessment Nov 30, 2025; CNN Dec 1, 2025). It has not resolved quickly or cleanly, aligning with the 'protracted' aspect. US and allies have committed massive aid (hundreds of billions), facing political fatigue and strategic debates, often described as a quagmire (e.g., *The Ukraine Quagmire*, Jul 2025; SCMP on US 'strategic quagmire', Jun 2025). While lacking US troop casualties like Vietnam (~58k dead) or Iraq (~4k), it mirrors the endless aid sink, stalled progress, and diplomatic exhaustion without victory. Peace talks under Trump (e.g., 28-point plan, Axios Nov 2025; Guardian Dec 1, 2025) show no resolution yet, validating Ramaswamy's prediction over quick victory narratives.
